'''Satyan L. Devadoss''' is the [[Fletcher Jones (American entrepreneur)|Fletcher Jones]] Professor of Applied Mathematics and Professor of Computer Science at the [[University of San Diego]].<ref name="cv">[http://www.satyandevadoss.org/s/devadossCV.pdf Curriculum vitae], retrieved September 1, 2021.</ref> His research concerns [[topology]] and [[geometry]], mostly seen through a discrete and computational lens, with inspiration coming from [[theoretical physics]], [[phylogenetics]], and [[scientific visualization]].

==Academia==
Devadoss graduated as valedictorian from [[North Central College]] in 1993.<ref name="cv"/> He earned his Ph.D. in mathematics in 1999 from [[Johns Hopkins University]], under the supervision of [[Jack Morava]].<ref name="cv"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=38246}}</ref> He was a Ross assistant professor at the [[Ohio State University]] under [[Ruth Charney]] and Mike Davis before joining the faculty at [[Williams College]], receiving tenure and promotion to full-professor.<ref name="cv"/>  He has held visiting positions at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], the [[Ohio State University]], [[Harvey Mudd College]], the [[University of California, San Diego]], the [[Mathematical Sciences Research Institute]], and [[Stanford University]].<ref name="cv"/>

==Awards==
Devadoss is a recipient of the Henry Alder National Teaching Award (2007), the Northeastern Sectional Award for Distinguished Teaching (2014), and a [[Deborah and Franklin Haimo Awards for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics|Deborah and Franklin Haimo Award for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics]] (2016),<ref name=web>{{Cite web|url=https://maa.org/member-communities/maa-awards/teaching-awards/section-award|title=Recipients of the Deborah and Franklin Tepper Haimo Award for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics; Mathematical Association of America|website=www.maa.org|access-date=October 7, 2024|archive-date=June 8, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240608175318/https://maa.org/member-communities/maa-awards/teaching-awards/section-award|url-status=dead}}</ref> all awarded by the [[Mathematical Association of America]].<ref>[http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/teaching-awards/henry-l-alder-award Henry L. Alder Award], MAA, retrieved January 16, 2015.</ref><ref>[https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/news/2007%20Prize%20Book.pdf MathFest 2007 Prizes and Awards], MAA, retrieved January 16, 2015.</ref>

In 2012, he became an inaugural [[Fellow]] of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180825194636/http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list |date=August 25, 2018 }}, retrieved January 16, 2015.</ref>

Devadoss has also received the Nelson Bushnell Prize (2012) from Williams College, the Young Alumni Award (2008) from North Central College, and the inaugural William Kelso Morrill Award (1995) from the Johns Hopkins University.<ref name="cv"/><ref>[https://www.northcentralcollege.edu/alumni-awards-2009-1995 NCC Alumni award winners]</ref><ref>[https://sites.krieger.jhu.edu/math-intranet/for-graduate-students/graduate-awards/ William Kelso Morrill Award winners]</ref>

==Works==
In 2017, Devadoss led a team at the University of San Diego to receive a $1M grant from the Fletcher Jones Foundation<ref>[https://www.fletcherjonesfdn.org Fletcher Jones Foundation]</ref> for the renovation of his mathematics department.  The centerpiece of this renovation was his Math Studio, a laboratory that focuses on the physical questions surrounding mathematics research.<ref>[https://www.sandiego.edu/news/detail.php?_focus=64627 USD news]</ref><ref>[https://www.sandiego.edu/news/detail.php?_focus=69535 USD news]</ref><ref>[https://timesofsandiego.com/education/2017/10/09/usd-gets-1m-grant-to-renovate-math-education-classroom-space/ Times of San Diego, 09-10-2017]</ref>

With [[Joseph O'Rourke (professor)|Joseph O'Rourke]], Devadoss is a coauthor of the textbook ''Discrete and Computational Geometry'' (Princeton University Press, 2011).<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Fasy | first1 = Brittany Terese | author1-link = Brittany Fasy
 | last2 = Millman | first2 = David L.
 | date = March 2014
 | doi = 10.1145/2596583.2596591
 | issue = 1
 | journal = SIGACT News
 | location = New York, NY, USA
 | pages = 27–30
 | publisher = ACM
 | title = Review of ''Discrete and Computational Geometry'' by Satyan L. Devadoss and Joseph O'Rourke
 | volume = 45| s2cid = 9912838
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation|first=Bill|last=Wood|title=Discrete and Computational Geometry|department=MAA Reviews|publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]|url=http://www.maa.org/publications/maa-reviews/discrete-and-computational-geometry|date=December 29, 2011}}.</ref>  With Matt Harvey, he is a coauthor of the tradebook ''Mage Merlin's Unsolved Mathematical Mysteries'' (MIT Press, 2020).<ref>[https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/mage-merlins-unsolved-mathematical-mysteries MIT Press]</ref>  Devadoss was also recruited by the [[Great Courses]] to create the ''Shape of Nature'', a 36-lecture video course focusing on the applications of geometry and topology to the natural world.<ref>[https://www.thegreatcourses.com/courses/shape-of-nature Great Courses]</ref>

He was a cofounder of CereusData, a data visualization company that focuses on storytelling of institutional data.<ref>[http://satyandevadoss.org/cereusdata CereusData], retrieved January 16, 2015.</ref>

Devadoss wrote opinion editorials published by the Chicago Tribune (2023) on mathematics and the machines<ref>[https://www.chicagotribune.com/opinion/commentary/ct-opinion-math-machines-artificial-intelligence-ai-lessons-20230921-agvg25banjfathcdavjenqzwbe-story.html Chicago Tribune oped, 09-21-2023]</ref> and by the Los Angeles Times (2021) on the tension between the usefulness and wonder of mathematics.<ref>[https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2021-08-22/mathematics-anxiety-phobia-students-algebra LA Times oped, 08-22-2021]</ref>  He also wrote an opinion editorial in the Washington Post (2018) on the nature of mathematics related to the humanities and the arts. It was chosen by the staff editors as one of their favorite opeds of the year.<ref>{{cite news |title=Opinion {{!}} Our favorite Washington Post op-eds of 2018 |date=December 18, 2018 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2018/12/18/our-favorite-washington-post-op-eds/?noredirect=on}}</ref><ref>
[https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/a-math-problem-for-pi-day/2018/03/14/7d562a78-27be-11e8-bc72-077aa4dab9ef_story.html?noredirect=on A math problem for Pi day]</ref>

==Artworks==
In 2018, he co-led a team in designing, creating, and showcasing a two-ton metal, wood, and acrylic interactive sculpture titled "Unfolding Humanity" for [[Burning Man]].<ref>[https://www.sandiego.edu/news/detail.php?_focus=70960 Making of "Unfolding Humanity"], retrieved February 13, 2019.</ref>  This sculpture made a return appearance to Burning Man in 2023 as a special Arts Honoraria project.<ref>[https://burningman.org/programs/burning-man-arts/ Burning Man Arts Grants], retrieved January 18, 2024.</ref> The 12-foot tall dodecahedral artwork, externally skinned with black panels containing 2240 acrylic windows, with the interior lined with mirrors and large enough to hold 15 people, dealt with unsolved questions in mathematics (unfolding polyhedra) and physics (cosmological shape of the universe).<ref>[https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201904/rnoti-p572.pdf Notices of the AMS cover article], retrieved April 25, 2019.</ref>

His collection of paintings, titled "Cartography of Tree Space" (jointly created with San Francisco-based artist Owen Schuh) has been on gallery shows in Berlin<ref>[http://www.satelliteberlin.org/pages/treespace SatelliteBerlin] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160301170013/http://www.satelliteberlin.org/pages/treespace |date=March 1, 2016 }}, retrieved January 15, 2016.</ref>  and Pasadena.<ref>[http://www.artcenter.edu/connect/events/uncertainty-exhibition.html Williamson Gallery], retrieved January 15, 2017.</ref><ref>[http://leonardo.info/blogs/uncertainty-exhibition-review/ Leonardo Uncertainty Review], retrieved February 1, 2016.</ref> As of 2023, the triptych of paintings is in the permanent collection of the Flaten Art Museum.
